name: Cognita
shortSummary: An educational software ecosystem exploring connected learning tools, educational resources, and school-focused digital workflows.
description: Cognita is an educational software project focused on bringing learning resources and digital tools into a more cohesive environment. The broader concept includes lessons, learning materials, sandboxes, and tools for teachers to manage educational content.
overview: An educational software ecosystem focused on connecting learning resources and digital tools.
Explores lessons, learning materials, sandboxes, and teacher-oriented content management.
Uses a modular approach to separate learning content from supporting educational tools.
Long-term direction includes integrated learning environments and structured digital workflows.
The overall platform remains under development, with planned capabilities distinguished from implemented functionality.
problem: Educational resources can be fragmented across separate tools and platforms
Learning materials need to remain associated with the lessons they support
Teachers need practical ways to organize and maintain digital learning content
features: Learning environments and sandbox module concept
stack: Additional framework and database choices depend on the specific module
architecture: Modular educational platform
Separate learning-content and teacher-facing workflows
Potential integration with dedicated learning environments
challenges: Defining clear boundaries between platform modules
Keeping lesson content and supporting materials connected
Distinguishing platform-wide functionality from module-specific functionality
lessons: Large educational platforms benefit from modular design
Content organization is a core part of the user experience
Product scope should be defined before individual modules are expanded
limitations: The broader platform concept is not a fully implemented production system
Some modules remain planned or exploratory
Deployment, integrations, and feature completeness vary by component
future: Develop the lesson and materials workflows
Implement teacher-facing lesson editing
Develop learning environments and sandbox integration
Define authentication, authorization, and platform-wide data management

name: Cognita-os
shortSummary: A Linux-based desktop shell concept for educational environments, built with C++20 and Qt 6.
description: Cognita OS is a custom Linux desktop shell project designed around the needs of educational environments. Rather than developing a new operating-system kernel, the project explores building a dedicated graphical environment on top of Linux, using Qt 6 and the Mir/Wayland ecosystem.
overview: A custom Linux desktop shell designed around the needs of educational environments.
Built on Linux rather than developing a new operating-system kernel.
Uses C++20, Qt 6, and CMake for its application and build foundation.
Explores the Mir and Wayland graphical ecosystem.
Current work focuses on the shell foundation, configuration, logging, and graphics integration.
The complete desktop experience remains a future development goal.
problem: General-purpose desktop environments may not match the requirements of a controlled school computing environment
A dedicated shell needs a maintainable foundation for future desktop components
Graphical environments must integrate correctly with Linux display and rendering infrastructure
architecture: Linux-based desktop shell rather than a custom kernel
ShellApplication separates application logic from the entry point
Configuration and logging components provide shared infrastructure
Mir and Wayland are part of the intended graphical-session architecture
challenges: Integrating Qt with the Linux graphical stack
Troubleshooting EGL, OpenGL, and software-rendering issues in a virtual machine
Establishing a stable build and dependency configuration
Separating the initial shell foundation from future desktop functionality
lessons: A working build does not guarantee a working graphical rendering pipeline
Graphics problems can originate in the environment and driver stack rather than application code
Separating application responsibilities makes future shell development easier
Display-server architecture needs to be understood before adding desktop features
limitations: The current implementation is an early shell prototype
The complete desktop interface is not implemented
Launcher, panel, notifications, settings, lock screen, and session-management functionality remain planned
Graphics and rendering issues have affected development
future: Resolve the current graphical rendering issues
Establish a reliable shell session using the intended Mir/Wayland setup
Implement the desktop panel and application launcher
Add settings, notifications, search, and session management
Explore integration with centralized school infrastructure

name: Quax — Tourism Platform
shortSummary: A collaborative tourism web application prototype built with Next.js, TypeScript, Prisma, and Supabase PostgreSQL.
description: Quax is a collaborative web application project focused on tourism and destination discovery. The project uses a modern TypeScript web stack and is scoped around an initial city or country experience rather than attempting to cover every destination at once.
overview: A collaborative tourism web application developed by a two-person team.
Focuses on destination discovery with an initially limited geographic scope.
Uses Next.js and TypeScript for the web application.
Uses Prisma for data access and Supabase PostgreSQL for relational data storage.
Explores full-stack application design, database modelling, and collaborative development.
The project is a prototype, with functionality and production readiness dependent on ongoing development.
problem: Tourism information can be spread across multiple websites and services
A broad destination platform needs a manageable initial scope
A collaborative application needs a clear division of implementation responsibilities
architecture: Full-stack web application using Next.js
TypeScript for application code
Prisma as the database access and data-modeling layer
Supabase PostgreSQL as the relational database
Two-person collaborative development
challenges: Defining a realistic minimum viable product
Coordinating changes between two developers
Maintaining consistency between application data models and the database
Keeping the initial product scope focused on a limited geographic area
lessons: A focused MVP is easier to design and validate than a broad platform
Clear task ownership helps collaborative development
Database schemas and application models need to evolve together
Full-stack projects require coordination between user experience, application logic, and persistence
limitations: The project is a prototype rather than a confirmed production service
The initial geographic scope is limited
Production readiness, deployment, and feature completeness have not been established
future: Complete and validate the initial destination experience
Refine the database schema and data-management workflows
Improve responsive design and usability
Add destinations and related tourism information
Document deployment and production requirements

name: Home Lab OPS
shortSummary: A collection of operational tools and self-hosted services for managing and monitoring a personal Linux home lab.
description: Home Lab OPS is an ongoing home-lab project focused on operating self-hosted services, managing server infrastructure, and developing tools for monitoring and administration. The environment includes an Ubuntu Server host, Docker-based services, Caddy, network file sharing, and hosted websites.
overview: An operational project focused on managing and maintaining a personal home-lab environment.
Runs on an Ubuntu Server host with Docker-based services.
Uses Caddy for reverse proxying and web hosting.
Includes Samba-based network file sharing and persistent server storage.
Uses Cloudflare for external access to selected services.
Includes development of a web-based dashboard for server administration and monitoring.
The dashboard and future operational capabilities are separate from the infrastructure already running.
problem: Self-hosted services require reliable configuration and persistent storage
Operating multiple services through separate tools can complicate administration
Publicly accessible services need controlled network exposure
Server administration benefits from a centralized operational overview
features: Caddy reverse proxy and web hosting
Cloudflare-based public access for selected services
Development of a server management dashboard
stack: C# for the related ServerMonitor prototype
architecture: Linux host running self-hosted infrastructure
Docker containers for selected services
Caddy reverse proxy for web traffic
Persistent application and service data stored on server storage
Samba for network file access
Cloudflare for selected external access paths
Separate dashboard and monitoring development
challenges: Configuring services to persist across restarts
Managing permissions across Linux users, storage, and network shares
Troubleshooting public access and tunnel availability
Maintaining existing websites while making infrastructure changes
Designing a dashboard without unnecessarily exposing administrative capabilities
lessons: Persistent storage and service configuration should be planned together
Reverse proxies and tunnels serve different roles in external access
Linux file permissions matter when accessing files through multiple services
Monitoring and administrative control should be designed as distinct capabilities
Infrastructure changes should be tested without disrupting running services
limitations: The server uses older, resource-constrained hardware

name: ServerMonitor
shortSummary: A C# monitoring prototype that collects Linux system metrics and exposes them as structured data.
description: ServerMonitor is a C# and .NET prototype for collecting system information from Linux. Its collectors inspect operating-system metrics such as CPU load, memory, network interfaces, storage, running processes, and host information. The project is intended to provide a foundation for a reusable monitoring component and future server-dashboard integration.
overview: A C# and .NET prototype for collecting Linux system metrics.
Separates collection responsibilities across CPU, memory, network, processes, storage, and system information.
Uses Linux interfaces such as /proc alongside .NET system APIs.
Produces structured, machine-readable metrics intended for integration with other tools.
Explores reusable monitoring components that could support the Home Lab OPS dashboard.
The current prototype still requires reliability improvements, including storage exception handling and optional sensor detection.
problem: Linux system metrics are exposed through different interfaces
Monitoring output needs a consistent structure for consumption by other applications
Some metrics may require permissions or may not be available on every machine
A dashboard needs machine-readable data rather than terminal-only output
features: Process information including PID and resource usage
Host, operating system, kernel, architecture, and uptime information
architecture: Separate collectors for CPU, memory, network, processes, storage, and system information
Collectors gather data from Linux system interfaces and .NET APIs
Metric results are designed for structured output
Potential integration with a separate server dashboard
challenges: Handling inaccessible storage paths and permission errors
Supporting systems without available hardware temperature sensors
Normalizing metrics from different operating-system sources
Distinguishing missing sensor data from actual system failures
Preventing a single collector failure from crashing the entire monitoring process
lessons: Operating-system metrics can have different availability and permission requirements
Hardware sensor availability should not be assumed
Collectors should handle errors independently where practical
Structured output makes system monitoring easier to integrate into other applications
A monitoring tool needs explicit handling for missing and invalid measurements
limitations: The prototype is not yet a fully reliable monitoring service
Hardware sensor detection is not working reliably in the current test environment
Storage collection has encountered an UnauthorizedAccessException
Metric accuracy and behavior across different Linux distributions require further testing
A complete dashboard integration is not yet established
future: Resolve storage collection permission and exception-handling issues
Improve optional sensor detection
Standardize JSON output and missing-value handling
Test collectors independently and across multiple Linux environments
Add automated tests for metric parsing and error conditions
Integrate the collectors with the Home Lab OPS dashboard
